title: Qualitative Market Research | Methods & Examples | CoLoop
summary: Read about core qualitative market research methods, from focus groups to ethnography. Learn how to uncover the motivation behind consumer behaviour.
body_markdown:
These days, businesses have a continuously increasing wealth of data. This information is undeniably useful for research, giving numbers and hard figures that tell you explicitly what your customers are doing. But it doesn’t explain why they’re doing it.


In fact, a[2026 Brandwatch survey of over 1,000 marketers](https://www.brandwatch.com/reports/marketer/) found that just 25% say they understand their audiences very well, and 40% name uncovering the “why” behind audience decisions as one of their biggest challenges.


This is where qualitative research comes into play, providing the motivations and opinions of your consumers that give meaning to their behaviour. You need both aspects of research — the figures and the feedback — to truly understand your audience and be able to make decisions that benefit them.


There are multiple methods of qualitative market research, which we’ll cover throughout this guide, that allow you to gather detailed, open-ended feedback that uncovers unmet needs and challenges your assumptions.


We’ll explore everything involved in collecting qualitative information, as well as the benefits of doing market research, and discuss how AI can be used to improve the process while still maintaining the rigour and accuracy that is required to produce meaningful insights.


## What Is Qualitative Market Research?


Qualitative market research aims to understand your customers’ opinions and why they act the way that they do. It uncovers the contextual information that can’t be presented numerically, such as:


- Consumer decisions: the drivers behind customer behaviour.
- Brand perception: how your audience views your business compared to your competitors.
- Product and service gaps: which of your customers’ needs or desires you’re currently not meeting.
- Emerging trends: how audience preferences are changing.


These insights come only from a genuine understanding of people’s mindsets, so qualitative market research methods need to be explorative and focused on digging beneath the surface. For this reason, it tends to use smaller sample sizes than quantitative research. But how else do these approaches differ?


## Qualitative Research vs Quantitative Research


The difference between qualitative and quantitative market research all comes down to what kind of insight you’re trying to gain.


Quantitative research collects numerical data that measures statistical conclusions about customers. This often includes purchase frequency, spending habits, sales volumes, and engagement rates. Put simply, it measures what customers are doing across your business. In contrast, qualitative research focuses on *why* customers are doing these things.


Both are equally important.


The variance doesn't lie only in their goals, however. The data type and sample size also differ. Quantitative research generates numerical data and benefits from large sample sizes to produce greater representation and easier comparisons, while qualitative research gathers descriptive, word-based data and tends to use smaller sample sizes to allow for in-depth conversations.


Here are the differences at a glance:


Quantitative research Qualitative research


Goal Measures behaviours and patterns Explores motivations and opinions


Data type Numerical data and statistics Descriptive data, including observations and accounts


Sample size Typically larger samples Typically smaller samples


Analysis Statistical analysis to identify trends and relationships Thematic and interpretative analysis to identify recurring ideas and deeper meaning


Though quantitative and qualitative research serve different purposes, this doesn’t mean it's a choice between one or the other. In fact, they work best together. Qualitative research fills the contextual gaps that quantitative data leaves behind, helping you understand the motivations behind the patterns you identify. Meanwhile, quantitative research can establish how widespread these findings are across a larger audience.


## What Are the Benefits of Qualitative Market Research?


We’ve established that your findings from qualitative research will help you understand your customer better, but how exactly will this benefit you (and them)?


### Informing Product Development


One thing that qualitative research excels at is uncovering unmet needs. Who better to tell you what they want than your customers themselves?


Focused interviews reveal what problems your customers are currently facing and where frustrations lie, giving you the opportunity to strategise ways to solve these with future products.


Similarly, qualitative research gives you an avenue to test early concepts and gain feedback on designs before investing in full development.


The stakes of getting this right are high, as only around[30%](https://nielseniq.com/global/en/insights/report/2026/launch-fast-learn-faster/) of new consumer goods reach 1% household penetration in their first year.


The right research ensures that your products continue to meet and exceed your audience’s expectations.


### Refining Marketing Strategies


Qualitative research reveals how customers think and talk about your products and brand. It allows you to discover what people relate to and what their motivations are.


This is marketing gold. With these insights, it becomes far easier to craft marketing messages that genuinely resonate with your intended audience, rather than relying on assumptions and hoping you hit the target.


Interviews reveal the words and phrases customers naturally use to describe their wants and needs, giving you the opportunity to mirror this language in campaigns to make them more relatable.


You can even[test creative concepts](https://www.coloop.ai/solutions#concept-stimulus-testing) and advertising messaging directly with the target audience to see which have the intended effect, and which don't, before publication.


### Identifying Emerging Trends


Consumer preferences and expectations are always evolving, and qualitative research helps you keep up or even get ahead by spotting changes before they become obvious in statistical market data.


Open-ended conversations give participants an avenue to discuss their changing needs in a way that wouldn’t be possible in a structured survey. Then, by analysing multiple responses, you can see recurring themes that may indicate a new trend.


These insights afford you a valuable opportunity to proactively respond, either by exploring new market opportunities or adapting your messaging to reflect new expectations.


### Inspiring Smarter Business Decisions


By nature, qualitative data is more human than other forms of information, as each response is an individual story. This makes the research findings more relatable, helping you connect to the people behind the data rather than only seeing numbers.


These personal experiences provide a clearer picture of how business decisions affect real people and make research findings easier to communicate and understand across teams. They can also help build empathy for customers, encouraging more thoughtful decisions that reflect their actual needs.


## Common Types of Qualitative Research


Although qualitative research always aims to explore the motivations and opinions of your customers, there are a few different ways to go about collecting them.


Here are the most common methodologies.


### Focus Groups


Focus groups are probably the most common form of qualitative market research.


A moderator poses questions to a small group of participants, listens to the dialogue, and explores the opinions and reactions.


Throughout the session, participants may also be asked to complete activities to help deepen discussion and allow you to extract further insights.


The advantage of focus groups is that shared discussions can uncover shared beliefs and social norms, making trends easier to identify.


These sessions can either be completed online or in-person. While in-person sessions are best for some use cases, such as testing product prototypes, remote focus groups offer more flexibility and access to a wider range of participants.


### In-Depth Interviews (IDIs)


In contrast to focus groups, in-depth interviews are a one-on-one qualitative research method. They involve individual conversations between a participant and a moderator with the aim of getting deep insights into their personal experiences and perspectives.


These discussions can take place in-person, over the phone, or via an online video call.


The benefit of IDIs is that they yield rich, individual perspectives without the interjection of group biases.


### Ethnographic Research


Ethnographic research differs a little from the previous two methods as it involves observing people in their natural environments rather than relying solely on discussions.


Instead of asking direct questions, researchers immerse themselves in the everyday lives of participants to understand how they authentically behave in real-world contexts. For instance, this could involve seeing how a customer uses a product at home.


Witnessing this firsthand exposes any habits or frustrations that the participant may not think to mention during an interview or focus group. Put simply, it helps you understand not just what people say they do, but what they actually do.


## The Qualitative Research Process


Qualitative research extends beyond just collecting descriptive data from participants; in fact, this is just one stage of the wider process.


Here, we’ve broken it down into six steps. End-to-end qualitative research platforms like CoLoop can support all the following steps.


### 1. Research Planning and Design


Before diving into the research itself, you should determine what exactly it is that you want to find out. Establish your objectives, define the questions you want to answer, and decide which research methods will best suit your aims.


At this point, you should also identify your target audience or participation criteria and plan a timeline for your project, as well as any resources you’ll need.


After all, a well-designed study gives the research direction and helps ensure the data collected answers the questions that matter.


### 2. Participant Recruitment and Preparation


Once you’ve designed your research, you’ll need people to actually take part. But not just anyone will do.


Participant selection is particularly important in qualitative research because the value of the findings depends heavily on whose experiences and opinions you explore. Therefore, you want to recruit those who represent relevant customer groups and have valuable perspectives to share.


Within this stage, you should also obtain informed consent from participants and prepare them for what’s involved, including organising any activities needed for the research.


### 3. Data Collection


Only after the previous two preparatory steps should you move on to interacting with participants and gathering qualitative data. Depending on the method you choose, this will involve either one-to-one interviews, focus groups, online discussions, or observing people in their natural environments.


To gather the most valuable data possible, ensure you’re asking open-ended questions and following up on interesting responses. Record conversations, document observations, and collect physical materials such as written feedback or video.


Although it’s vital to be prepared, you should also be willing to adapt, bringing in additional questions as new themes or ideas emerge. Sometimes unexpected avenues deliver the deepest insights.


### 4. Data Preparation and Organisation


When conducting the multiple interviews and focus groups that qualitative research demands, you inevitably end up with substantial amounts of unstructured data, from recordings and notes to written feedback and diaries.


Before analysis, you need to organise all this information into a consistent format. This usually requires transcribing discussions and checking these transcripts for accuracy, as well as anonymising personal information where appropriate.


Also, it’s often useful at this stage to group data by topic or participant type.


Well-organised data makes the subsequent analysis more manageable and helps retain context.


### 5. Data Analysis


With the research conducted, you can now begin extracting insights from your data. This often involves thematic analysis, where you examine the data to identify recurring ideas, behaviours, concerns, and motivations.


During the analysis process, you should look to:


- Code responses and identify recurring themes.
- Compare perspectives across different participants or audience groups.
- Explore contradictions, unusual responses, and outliers.
- Identify relationships between different themes.
- Support interpretations with direct participant quotes and evidence.
- Draw conclusions that address the original research objectives.


At this stage, accuracy is essential. Any conclusions you draw should be[backed by specific evidence](https://www.coloop.ai/features#evidence-panel) rather than assumptions.


### 6. Reporting


The final stage involves communicating the findings in a way that helps stakeholders understand what the research reveals and what they can do with that information. Even excellent research has limited value if its findings aren't communicated clearly or connected to business decisions. This is what turns research into a practical resource.


So, how do you do it? One aspect is to highlight key themes and findings, connecting these clearly to your original research objectives. These should be backed up by specific quotes and examples, and complement recommendations for resulting action in either product design, marketing, or wider strategy.


## How Do Qualitative Market Research Companies Implement AI Effectively?


Some aspects of qualitative research can be time-consuming and error-prone, particularly when you’re transcribing multiple conversations (perhaps translating across languages) and then trying to identify themes.


[AI makes the process far more manageable](https://www.coloop.ai/blog/how-ai-assists-qualitative-data-analysis) , with the capability to achieve much of this work automatically.


At this point, the risks are probably springing to mind. AI may improve efficiency, but qualitative research relies on accuracy and evidence to produce genuinely meaningful insights. Common AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude, though undeniably useful, are infamous for their hallucinations and struggles with understanding context.


That’s why CoLoop uses its own research-grade AI to complement these tools, producing trusted insights that you can then explore further with general artificial intelligence.


This supports fast transcription, translation, thematic analysis, categorisation, and reporting, while also:


### Grounding Findings in Actual Research Evidence


General-use AI tools might quickly generate summaries and[‘fast-food’ insights](https://www.coloop.ai/blog/fast-food-research-ai-insights-qual360-berlin-2026) that sound convincing, but their findings may not accurately reflect the original research. AI used for research should ground analysis in your data and allow you to check the evidence behind every conclusion.


### Preserving Context and Nuance


The meaning behind responses is critical when drawing conclusions from qualitative research, so simply counting how often particular words or topics appear won't cut it.


AI needs to account for this context rather than making broad assumptions, identifying recurring patterns while also retaining individual perspectives.


### Maintaining Human Oversight


AI responses can’t be trusted as always correct, so being able to see how conclusions were reached is essential. A research-grade AI tool links its interpretations back to the original research materials so a human in the loop can verify participant quotes, ensure nothing has been taken out of context, and explore alternative interpretations. This also maintains human responsibility for the final conclusions and recommendations.

### Making Insights Reusable


Qualitative research shouldn't become redundant as soon as a project ends, but unfortunately this is often the case. Prior research gets forgotten about or lost, causing wasted work that ends up being repeated. Research-grade AI builds a searchable repository of findings that allows you to compare past findings with current ones.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### How many participants do you need for qualitative market research?


There’s no fixed number of participants needed for qualitative research, but a general guide to follow is the concept of *data saturation* , where you continue additional interviews or discussions until they stop adding anything meaningful. Often, a smaller, carefully selected sample can be more valuable than a much larger, less targeted one.


### How can you reduce bias in qualitative market research?


Bias is an ethical concern in qualitative research, but you can reduce or avoid it with careful research design. Use neutral, open-ended questions and recruit participants with a range of relevant perspectives. Then, during analysis, consider contradictory responses and actively look for evidence that challenges your initial assumptions.


### How can qualitative researchers protect participant data when using AI?


Security and privacy are concerns in any activity involving data, and qualitative research is no exception. Researchers should consider how participant information is collected, stored, processed, and used by AI. This includes checking data retention policies and access permissions, among other security best practices.
